steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an NLP paper about using natural language "standing instructions" (preferences the user states once) as extra context when a task-oriented assistant interprets user requests. Cover the motivation, how it relates to prior work, and our dataset and contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs with tools/APIs and the need to respect user preferences
- Limits of learning preferences implicitly
- Proposal: standing instructions as explicit context
- Related work: developer guidelines, system prompts / custom instructions
- Contributions: NLSI dataset, reasoning types, benchmarking

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs with tools/APIs and user preferences
  - LLMs (GPT-3, GPT-4, LLaMa 2) increasingly used with tools and APIs (cite) for extra functionality
  - e.g. ChatGPT external plugins: OpenTable for searching/reserving restaurants, Expedia for travel
  - apps must identify which service user wants + respect preferences across diverse domains, unique per user
  - preferences -> personalisation: tailored responses, more accurate recommendations, saves user time
  - but users usually verbalise preferences in detail during interaction, even for repeated requests
- Learning preferences implicitly
  - past work: learn preferences from user-system interactions over time (cite)
  - hard to learn, needs lots of training data
  - implicit -> usually not interpretable or editable by user
- Proposal: standing instructions
  - personalised standing instructions as explicit additional context when interpreting requests
  - definition: user-provided NL statements that change/prescribe system behaviour under certain circumstances
  - Fig. 1: user looks for nearby restaurants; without SIs, multiple turns to get to cuisine + location
  - with relevant SIs: search Persian restaurants in San Leandro directly; saves time, customised/localised recs
  - controllable + interpretable; user can inspect/edit, esp. preferences that change over time
  - outputs linked to relevant SIs -> user trust (cite)
- Related work
  - closest: work conditioning dialogue model response on developer guidelines (cite)
  - open-domain dialogue, response generation; reducing toxicity, safety
  - commercial LLM providers: System Prompts / Custom Instructions / Preamble -> guidelines at start of every conversation
  - little known about how it works, no documented evaluations, esp. task-oriented setting
- Contributions
  - (i) systematic study in task-oriented setup; NLSI (Natural Language Standing Instructions) dataset, English
    - example = user-agent conversation + standing instructions (user profile) + sequence of API calls (user intents)
  - (ii) six reasoning types: single instruction for one attribute ... multiple preferences for same aspect
    - challenges: selecting subset of relevant SIs, inferring structured API calls + arguments
    - single preference up to multi-hop, cross-domain, conflict reasoning
  - (iii) benchmark methods for selection + interpretation; LLM-based methods far from perfect
    - new challenges: retrieval, reasoning, semantic parsing

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) like GPT-3, GPT-4 and LLaMa 2 are now more and more used together with tools and APIs so that they can give users extra functionality. For example, ChatGPT lets you use several external plugins, like OpenTable to search for and reserve restaurants, or Expedia to book travel. These applications have to figure out which service the user wants, and they also have to respect the user's preferences, which are spread over many different domains and are unique to each user. If the system understands these preferences it can personalise the experience, with tailored responses, more accurate recommendations and less of the user's time spent. But in most cases the user has to say their preferences in detail during the interaction, and this is true even when the request is a repeated one.

Some past work has looked at learning preferences from the interactions between the user and the system over time. But these preferences can be hard to learn and they also need a lot of training data. Also, the learnt preferences are implicit, so usually the user cannot interpret them or edit them.

We propose to add personalised standing instructions explicitly as extra context when the system interprets a user's requests. Standing instructions are natural language statements given by the user that change or prescribe how the system behaves under certain circumstances. For example, in Fig. 1 the user wants to look for some restaurants nearby. Without standing instructions, the user might have to go through multiple turns with the system before getting to the cuisine and location they prefer. If the system looks up the relevant standing instructions for restaurants, it can search for Persian restaurants in San Leandro directly, which saves the user time and also gives customised/localised recommendations. Explicit natural language instructions are also controllable and interpretable. The user can look at their standing instructions and edit them, especially for preferences that change over time. And the outputs that are generated can be linked directly to the relevant standing instructions, which makes the user trust the system more.

- Related work
  - closest: work conditioning dialogue model response on developer guidelines (cite)
  - open-domain dialogue, response generation; reducing toxicity, safety
  - commercial LLM providers: System Prompts / Custom Instructions / Preamble -> guidelines at start of every conversation
  - little known about how it works, no documented evaluations, esp. task-oriented setting

- Contributions
  - (i) systematic study in task-oriented setup; NLSI (Natural Language Standing Instructions) dataset, English
    - example = user-agent conversation + standing instructions (user profile) + sequence of API calls (user intents)
  - (ii) six reasoning types: single instruction for one attribute ... multiple preferences for same aspect
    - challenges: selecting subset of relevant SIs, inferring structured API calls + arguments
    - single preference up to multi-hop, cross-domain, conflict reasoning
  - (iii) benchmark methods for selection + interpretation; LLM-based methods far from perfect
    - new challenges: retrieval, reasoning, semantic parsing

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) like GPT-3, GPT-4 and LLaMa 2 are now more and more used together with tools and APIs so that they can give users extra functionality. For example, ChatGPT lets you use several external plugins, like OpenTable to search for and reserve restaurants, or Expedia to book travel. These applications have to figure out which service the user wants, and they also have to respect the user's preferences, which are spread over many different domains and are unique to each user. If the system understands these preferences it can personalise the experience, with tailored responses, more accurate recommendations and less of the user's time spent. But in most cases the user has to say their preferences in detail during the interaction, and this is true even when the request is a repeated one.

Some past work has looked at learning preferences from the interactions between the user and the system over time. But these preferences can be hard to learn and they also need a lot of training data. Also, the learnt preferences are implicit, so usually the user cannot interpret them or edit them.

We propose to add personalised standing instructions explicitly as extra context when the system interprets a user's requests. Standing instructions are natural language statements given by the user that change or prescribe how the system behaves under certain circumstances. For example, in Fig. 1 the user wants to look for some restaurants nearby. Without standing instructions, the user might have to go through multiple turns with the system before getting to the cuisine and location they prefer. If the system looks up the relevant standing instructions for restaurants, it can search for Persian restaurants in San Leandro directly, which saves the user time and also gives customised/localised recommendations. Explicit natural language instructions are also controllable and interpretable. The user can look at their standing instructions and edit them, especially for preferences that change over time. And the outputs that are generated can be linked directly to the relevant standing instructions, which makes the user trust the system more.

Our work is related to earlier work, which conditions the response of a dialogue model on a set of developer guidelines. That work is about controlling response generation in open-domain dialogue systems, mainly to reduce toxicity and make the systems safer. More recently, commercial LLM providers have added System Prompts / Custom Instructions / Preamble, which give an option to put guidelines at the start of every conversation so that response generation is better. However, not much is known about how this works, and there are no documented evaluations of how it is used, especially in the task-oriented setting.

The contributions of this work are: (i) We study in a systematic way how to incorporate standing instructions in a task-oriented setup. We develop and introduce NLSI (Natural Language Standing Instructions), an English-language dataset where each example has a conversation between the user and a dialogue agent, together with a collection of standing instructions (the user profile) and a sequence of API calls that reflect the user intents. (ii) We look at six reasoning types for using standing instructions, which go from a single instruction for a specific attribute to more complex situations like the user giving multiple preferences for the same aspect, etc. These reasoning types bring challenges in selecting the subset of relevant standing instructions and then in inferring the structured API calls and their arguments. They include instructions that specify a single preference and also more complex ones that need multi-hop, cross-domain and conflict reasoning. (iii) We use the dataset to benchmark a variety of methods for selecting and interpreting user utterances when standing instructions are present. We see that our LLM-based methods are far from perfect, which raises new challenges in retrieval, reasoning and semantic parsing.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-3 [1], GPT-4 [2], and LLaMa 2 [3] are increasingly being used with tools and APIs [4,5] to give users additional functionality. For example, ChatGPT allows several external plugins, such as OpenTable for searching and reserving restaurants or booking travel through Expedia. These applications must learn to identify which service the user is looking for while respecting preferences across diverse domains that are unique to each user. Understanding such preferences can help personalise the user experience through tailored responses, more accurate recommendations and time saved for the user. However, in most cases users must verbalise their preferences in detail during the interaction, even for repeated requests.

Past work has explored learning preferences from user-system interactions over time [6,7]. Such preferences can be hard to learn and also require significant amounts of training data. Further, these learnt preferences are implicit and usually cannot be interpreted or edited by the user.

We propose incorporating personalised standing instructions explicitly as additional context when interpreting a user’s requests. Standing instructions are user-provided natural language statements that change or prescribe system behaviour under certain circumstances. For example, in Fig. 1, the user wants to look for some nearby restaurants. Without standing instructions, the user might have to interact with the system for multiple turns to arrive at their preferred restaurant cuisine and location. By looking up the relevant standing instructions for restaurants, the system can directly search for Persian restaurants in San Leandro, saving the user’s time while also providing customised/localised recommendations. Explicit natural language instructions are also both controllable and interpretable. A user can inspect and edit their standing instructions, especially for preferences that change over time. Further, the generated outputs can be linked directly to the relevant standing instructions, which improves the user’s trust in the system [8].

Our work is related to [9], which conditions a dialogue model’s response on a set of developer guidelines. That work focuses on controlling response generation in open-domain dialogue systems, with the aim of reducing toxicity and enhancing safety. More recently, commercial LLM providers have introduced System Prompts /Custom Instructions /Preamble, which offer an option to include guidelines at the beginning of every conversation to improve response generation. However, little is known about how this operates, and no evaluations of its usage have been documented, especially in the task-oriented setting.

This work makes the following contributions: (i) We systematically study the incorporation of standing instructions in a task-oriented setup. We develop and introduce NLSI (Natural Language Standing Instructions), an English-language dataset in which each example consists of a conversation between the user and a dialogue agent, together with a collection of standing instructions (user profile) and a sequence of API calls reflecting user intents. (ii) We investigate six reasoning types for using standing instructions, ranging from a single instruction for a specific attribute to more complex situations such as the user proposing multiple preferences for the same aspect, etc. These reasoning types introduce challenges in selecting the subset of relevant standing instructions and then inferring the structured API calls and their arguments. They include instructions that specify a single preference as well as more complex ones involving multi-hop, cross-domain, and conflict reasoning. (iii) We use this dataset to benchmark a variety of methods for selecting and interpreting user utterances in the presence of standing instructions. We find that our LLM-based methods are far from perfect, which raises new challenges in retrieval, reasoning, and semantic parsing.
